extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and trainee reporters (particularly city/police beat reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Examples and illustrative pieces showing techniques for reporting police/crime stories and crime-related human-interest features, including straight crime leads, roundups, scene-setting narrative, and victim/suspect backgrounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual lead answering who/what/where/when
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the story with the principal fact(s): who was involved, what happened, where and when — stated plainly and early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by: “Walter H. Hammond... was shot and instantly killed yesterday afternoon in the Pennsylvania Railroad Company's ferry house at Jersey City.” Use a concise opening sentence that places the principal event up front so readers immediately know the core fact of the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include suspect/arrest details and official attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the suspect's name (if known), arrest status, and any statements or positions attributed to police or officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the account that “Peter Grew... was arrested as the slayer” and reporting of police statements such as Grew's alleged threats and drinking. Use clear attribution phrases (police say, he said, Amann says) and report whether the suspect admits guilt or refuses to answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide victim background and institutional identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Give readers contextual details about the victim: age, occupation, business/club affiliations, home address — facts that situate the victim socially and economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown by listing Hammond's business, directorships, club membership and home address. Such specifics help readers understand who the victim was and why the incident matters locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene description and immediate aftermath (witnesses, injuries, hospital status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the physical scene, damage, crowd reactions and the immediate condition/treatment of the injured or dying, including hospital transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: scattered pieces of hats and clothing on a car, women not revived, a hurry call to Lebanon Hospital, and Dr. Singer treating victims. Include who tended the wounded, where they were taken, and current condition (e.g., 'in a dangerous hysterical condition').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use witness, bystander and family quotations for color and human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate direct quotes from witnesses, bystanders, relatives (e.g., mothers) to add immediacy, character, and emotional perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful exemplars include the long, quoted account of Gene Sheehan's mother describing her son, the details she provides, and her emotional responses. Use such quotes to humanize victims and illuminate motive or community impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative/feature scene-setting for dramatic crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, structure the piece as a short narrative: open on action or a vivid scene, follow with the killing or key event, then broaden out to context and aftermath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by the Montclair shooting account: vivid running flight, sensory detail, and a dramatized climax. This style uses present-tense immediacy and descriptive detail to engage readers beyond a straight news lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roundup/chronicle format for multiple incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering many related crimes (e.g., a spate of murders in a neighborhood), present them as a dated list or chronicle, then analyze patterns or policing implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown in 'MURDER IN LITTLE ITALY Since January 1' which lists dates and short summaries of killings. Follow the list with synthesis (e.g., police staffing figures) to explain the pattern and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual reporting: policing, statistics and systemic factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Place incidents within broader institutional or systemic context — police staffing, patrol patterns, or local conditions that help explain why crimes occur or remain unsolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: quoting the chief of detectives about insufficient night patrols and providing department statistics (‘In all Kansas City there are only 264 patrolmen’). Use such context to move from incident reporting to analysis of causes or policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document prior history and motive allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report relevant past incidents, criminal records, civil disputes, or personal grievances that might bear on motive, while distinguishing allegations from proven facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reporting Grew's prior arrest for selling oleomargarine, his business decline, complaints about his wife, and his alleged threats. Use cautious attribution language for allegations and avoid presenting unproven motives as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localizing specifics (streets, addresses, beats) to anchor reportage
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor stories with precise local identifiers — street names, station names, beats, addresses — so readers can place events geographically and appreciate local relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories repeatedly use exact addresses (e.g., 'No. 314 Harrison avenue') and beat/station references. Accurate localization supports public interest and future follow-up reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of clear headings and sourcing labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Label dispatches with the originating paper or dateline and use section headings (e.g., 'MURDER', 'POLICE NEWS AND CRIME') to clarify genre and sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page shows multiple items headed with source names (New York Tribune, Kansas City Star) and topical headings. Proper labels help readers assess origin and category of each item.
